title: ₹1,300 Crore Wasn't Enough. Dhurandhar Just Landed in Japan.
excerpt: Ranveer Singh's spy saga adds Tokyo to a global conquest already spanning Toronto to Sydney — and Aamir Khan's all-time crown is starting to look reachable.
body:
A new poster dropped this week with **Dhurandhar**'s title rendered in bold Japanese kanji, and if that image doesn't capture exactly where Indian cinema stands in July 2026, nothing does. The Ranveer Singh-led spy thriller — already the fifth-highest-grossing Indian film of all time at ₹1,307 crore worldwide — will open in theatres across Japan on July 10, extending a global rampage that hasn't slowed since its December 2025 debut.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=BKOVzHcjEIo</youtube>

Ranveer recorded a special video message for Japanese audiences ahead of the release, calling the film an "immersive cinematic spectacle" and inviting viewers to experience the high-octane thriller on the biggest screen they can find. It's the kind of measured star diplomacy that signals real ambition — this isn't a token international release. The makers want Japan.

## The Numbers That Keep Getting Bigger

The franchise math is genuinely absurd. **Dhurandhar** (Part 1) holds the fifth spot on the all-time global chart with ₹1,307 crore. Its sequel, **Dhurandhar 2: The Revenge**, launched in March 2026 and currently sits third at ₹1,780 crore — within touching distance of overtaking **Baahubali 2: The Conclusion** for the number-two position. Between them, director **Aditya Dhar**'s two films occupy two of the top five slots in the history of Indian cinema. Two. Out of five.

The combined total of the franchise now exceeds ₹3,000 crore worldwide. The only target left worth chasing is Aamir Khan's **Dangal** at ₹2,070 crore — the all-time number one for a single Indian film. The Japan release opens a window, however slim, for the first chapter to chip away at that gap. Japan has become a surprisingly receptive market for Indian blockbusters: **RRR**, **Baahubali**, **Pushpa 2: The Rule**, and Ranbir Kapoor's **Animal** have all found theatrical audiences there in recent years.

## Global Domination, GCC Ban and All

What makes the Dhurandhar story extraordinary isn't just the gross — it's *where* the money came from. The film was **banned across six Gulf Cooperation Council nations**, cutting off one of Bollywood's most reliable overseas territories. And it didn't matter. Dhurandhar became the **number-one Hindi film of all time in North America**, the **highest-grossing Indian film ever in Canada and Australia**, and a top performer in the UK.

The story — Ranveer as an undercover Indian intelligence operative infiltrating Karachi's criminal syndicates and political corridors, tracing threads back to the 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks — was always going to be geopolitically charged. The GCC ban was predictable. What wasn't predictable was the film succeeding this spectacularly without those markets.

> "Dhurandhar is an immersive cinematic spectacle. I can't wait for Japan to experience it on the big screen." — Ranveer Singh

## Why Diaspora Audiences Should Care

If you're in the US, UK, or Canada and somehow haven't seen **Dhurandhar** yet — first of all, how? The film's theatrical run in diaspora markets was enormous. It dominated screens in cities with significant Indian populations and became a communal event in a way that only a handful of Bollywood films manage each decade.

The Japan release matters for diaspora audiences not because they'll fly to Tokyo to watch it, but because it represents something they've been asking for: Indian cinema being treated as global cinema. Not as a niche. Not as a curiosity. As a theatrical event worthy of dubbed releases and proper marketing campaigns in non-traditional territories.

The ensemble cast — **Akshaye Khanna**, **Sanjay Dutt**, **R. Madhavan**, **Arjun Rampal**, **Sara Arjun**, and scene-stealing **Rakesh Bedi** — delivered career-defining work, and the film's blend of espionage, patriotism, and raw emotion landed with audiences in a way that transcended language and borders.

## What's Next

With the Japan release, the Dhurandhar franchise is playing a longer game. Build the brand in new territories now. Let Part 1 establish the audience. When Part 2 inevitably follows into Japan (and potentially China, the last great untapped market), the floor is already set. Dangal's ₹2,070 crore record may feel safe today, but with every new territory, it gets a little less so.

Ranveer Singh turned 41 this year. He's entering the most commercially dominant stretch of any Bollywood leading man since Shah Rukh Khan's mid-2000s peak. And on July 10, he'll be introducing himself to Japan not as an actor, but as a franchise.
